You do realize that ISPs, like telcomm's, enjoy an exemption from the normal anti-monopoly rules. The ISPs, by and large, have collaborated (illegally, behind the scenes) to split up the country into territories and charge similar rates so that their competition doesn't cut into profits. As a result we find that ISPs use fairly homogeneous pricing structures and that most areas have woefully little in the way of choice or competition for ISP's.

In fact, smaller companies, (Like one a person would start, as you have suggested), are often unable to string their own wires, whether due to the staggering initial cost or the difficult nature of getting permits to do so, and quite frequently end up having to use the wires of the company that provided the poor service in the beginning.
Then end the exemptions! "Fixing" a broken law by making it even more broken is just stupid. Treat ISPs like every other business and the free market will surely fix all problems.

I'm actually open to this approach to a degree, though it's far more nuanced than that law alone. There are a number of unique legal issues surrounding the ISPs. For example, large ISP's currently do have to let smaller competitors use their wires, but they can make exploitative deals that take advantage of the smaller companies in some ways. There are other issues at hand that would make detangling the anti-monopoly exemption a little trickier (Including the question of how many new sets of wires do we want to have strung along our streets if there are suddenly a dozen competitors with their own wiring?) but if it were done in a way that allowed for the little guy to start up and compete, I'd be all for opening the market up to competition and seeing what happens.

Right now the only real example to point to there is the effect of Google Fiber coming to an area, which ususally forces a sudden decrease in price and increase in speed from the exisiting ISPs. That does show significant favor to the idea of competition being a better regulating factor when it comes to pricing and speed than what we've currently seen. At the same time, that effect also shows that the few ISPs to service an area have likely been collaborating behind the scenes to inflate prices and put off infrastructure upgrades in ways that bring them profit. That they so ably colluded in this way, and continue to do so, points out that the risk of them doing the same on content is just as likely. It would start off under the guide of 'protecting' people at first, but that's always a slippery slope, and as we've seen with speed and pricing, content censorship would be abused for profit. Whether it's blocking the content of competing services (Netflix, as a prime example), or censoring information to sanitize the available record of a government, corporation, or individual, it will be abused. The only way to stay off of it is to ensure the freedom of speech/content/access on the Internet, and that is where net neutrality becomes important.
